2 2. Criticality Meeting (July 28)
Source: Obsidian (July 28 Criticality Meeting.md).

2.1 Key Takeaway: Subformula Simplification vs. CDT Depth

A subformula simplifying to a single literal and its CDT having depth 1 are not the same thing.
Consider: \[F = (x_1 \vee x_2) \wedge (x_3 \vee x_4)\] If \(x_2 = 0\), the subformula \(F_1 = (x_1 \vee x_2)\) becomes \(x_1\). Its CDT has depth 1. But for the full formula \(F\), evaluating \(x_1\) does not terminate evaluation if \(x_1 = 1\); it forces exploration into \(F_2\).
Impact: Any inductive hypothesis that assumes depth scales additively with subformula depth must account for the gate connective and whether the subformula’s value determines the parent gate.

3 3. Discussion on Random Projections & Shrinkage
Source: Obsidian (Shrinkage under random projections.md).

Håstad [1998]: Established \(O(p^2)\) shrinkage under random restrictions for DeMorgan formulae, proving an \(\tilde{\Omega}(n^3)\) formula size lower bound for Andreev’s function.
Connection to Criticality: Proving \(\Gamma(F) = O(p\sqrt{L})\) would give tight average sensitivity bounds, improving Fourier concentration and learning algorithms for DeMorgan formulae.

title: Criticality of DeMorgan Formulae: Research Compilation
text:
This repository unifies and categorizes all working notes, proof attempts, counterexamples, and drafts from Obsidian, Notion, and Overleaf regarding the Criticality of DeMorgan Formulae.
The primary objective is to prove Tal’s Conjecture on the average sensitivity / decision tree depth of DeMorgan formulae under random restrictions:






Tal’s Conjecture



Let \(F\) be a DeMorgan formula of size \(L\) computing a Boolean function \(f: \{0,1\}^n \to \{0,1\}\). Under a \(p\)-random restriction \(\rho \sim \mathcal{R}_p\), does the decision tree depth of the restricted formula satisfy: \[\Pr_{\rho \sim \mathcal{R}_p} [\mathrm{DT}_{\mathrm{depth}}(F|_\rho) \ge t] \le (O(p \cdot \lambda))^t\] for some factor \(\lambda\) depending on formula structure (conjectured \(\lambda = O(\sqrt{L})\)), implying an average sensitivity / criticality bound of \(\Gamma(F) = O(p \sqrt{L})\)?

title: Working Manuscript Synthesis
section: 2 1. Canonical Decision Tree Construction with Balancing
text:
2 1. Canonical Decision Tree Construction with Balancing
Given a DeMorgan formula \(F\) over variable set \(V\) and a restriction \(\rho \in \{0, 1, *\}^V\), \(\mathrm{CDT}(F, \rho)\) is defined recursively:

2.1 Base Cases

If \(F \equiv 0\) or \(F \equiv 1\) under \(\rho\), \(\mathrm{CDT}(F, \rho)\) is a single leaf node labeled with the corresponding constant.
If \(F = \ell\) (a literal) and \(\rho(\mathrm{var}(\ell)) = *\), \(\mathrm{CDT}(F, \rho)\) queries \(\mathrm{var}(\ell)\) with two child leaves \(0\) and \(1\).



2.2 Recursive Merging and Simultaneous Balancing
Let \(F = F_1 \vee F_2\): 1. Recursively compute \(T_1 = \mathrm{CDT}(F_1, \rho)\). 2. For each leaf \(u\) of \(T_1\): - Let \(\pi_u\) denote the partial assignment corresponding to the path from the root of \(T_1\) to \(u\). - If \(T_1(u) = 1\), the OR gate is satisfied: the leaf remains labeled \(1\). - If \(T_1(u) = 0\), replace leaf \(u\) with \(\mathrm{Balance}(\mathrm{CDT}(F_2, \rho \circ \pi_u))\). 3. Apply global tree balancing \(\mathrm{Balance}(T)\) to ensure symmetry between \(0\)-paths and \(1\)-paths.

title: Working Manuscript Synthesis
section: 3 2. Structural Lemma: Blaming the Event on Subtrees
text:
3 2. Structural Lemma: Blaming the Event on Subtrees
Theorem (Structural Subtree Blame):
Let \(F\) be a DeMorgan formula and \(\rho \sim \mathcal{R}_p\). The bad event that \(\mathrm{CDT}_{\mathrm{depth}}(F|_\rho) \ge t\) can be covered by a union of events indexed by leaf-branching binary trees \(T\) with \(t\) leaves:
\[\Pr_{\rho \sim \mathcal{R}_p} [\mathrm{CDT}_{\mathrm{depth}}(F|_\rho) \ge t] \le \sum_{T \in \mathcal{T}_t} \sum_{b \in \{0,1\}^t} \Pr[\mathcal{E}(T, b)]\]
where for each pair \((T,b)\): \[\mathcal{E}(T, b) = \mathcal{A}(T, b) \wedge \mathcal{B}(T, b)\]
Here, \(\mathcal{A}(T, b)\) enforces that the internal routing conditions of \(T\) are satisfied, and \(\mathcal{B}(T, b)\) enforces that all \(t\) leaves simultaneously fall into the active restriction set (\(*\)).

3.1 Cauchy-Schwarz Bounding
By applying Cauchy-Schwarz: \[\Pr[\mathcal{E}(T, b)] \le \sqrt{\Pr[\mathcal{A}(T, b)] \cdot \Pr[\mathcal{B}(T, b)]}\]
Since \(\Pr[\mathcal{B}(T, b)] \le p^t\) (each leaf variable must be unassigned by \(\rho\)), the probability scales as: \[\Pr[\mathrm{CDT}_{\mathrm{depth}}(F|_\rho) \ge t] \le p^{t/2} \sum_{T \in \mathcal{T}_t} \sqrt{\Pr[\mathcal{A}(T, b)]}\]
The critical challenge is establishing that \(\sum_{T} \sqrt{\Pr[\mathcal{A}(T,b)]} \le (O(\sqrt{L}))^t\).

title: Taxonomy of Proof Approaches
text:
2 1. CDT with Simultaneous Balancing
Sources: Notion (New CDT.md, CDT with balancing.md), Overleaf (contents.tex, lines 240–350).
Status: Active
Key Idea: A primary flaw of naive Canonical Decision Trees is path asymmetry: a \(0\)-path in \(F_1\) may explore variables without guaranteeing a corresponding \(1\)-path over the same variable set. The Balancing operation ensures that for every explored node, the tree is balanced so that both \(0\) and \(1\) outcomes explore symmetric sets of variables or terminate simultaneously.






Simultaneous 0- and 1-Balancing



Given a decision tree \(T\), \(\mathrm{Balance}(T)\) recursively aligns branches: - If a subformula simplifies to a constant under path \(\pi\), redundant branches are pruned. - When merging \(\mathrm{CDT}(F_1, \rho)\) with \(\mathrm{CDT}(F_2, \rho \circ \pi)\), balancing is applied immediately at the point of creation rather than lazily when attached.


Current Hurdle:
Tracking path variables \(\mathrm{PathVars}(T)\) through multiple nested balancing steps complicates the inductive distribution under random restrictions \(\mathcal{R}_p\).

title: Taxonomy of Proof Approaches
section: 3 2. Non-Inductive Structural Lemma (Blaming Bad Events on Subtrees)
text:
3 2. Non-Inductive Structural Lemma (Blaming Bad Events on Subtrees)
Sources: Notion (New Proof.md, Rigorous proof.md), Overleaf (non-inductive proof.tex).
Status: Active
Key Idea: Rather than inducting step-by-step on \(t\), we bound \(\Pr[\mathrm{CDT}_{\mathrm{depth}}(F|_\rho) \ge t]\) globally: 1. Partition the bad event into \(\mathcal{E}(\bar{x}, a) = \{\rho : \mathrm{CDT}^{(a)}(F, \rho) = (x_{i_1}, \dots, x_{i_t})\}\). 2. Blame each bad sequence on a leaf-branching subtree \((T, b)\). 3. Factor the probability into \(\mathcal{E}(T, b) = \mathcal{A}(T, b) \wedge \mathcal{B}(T, b)\), where \(\mathcal{A}\) and \(\mathcal{B}\) represent independent or quasi-independent boundary conditions. 4. Apply Cauchy-Schwarz: \[\Pr[\mathcal{E}(\bar{x}, a)] \le \sum_{(T,b)} \sqrt{\Pr[\mathcal{A}(T,b)] \cdot \Pr[\mathcal{B}(T,b)]}.\]
Current Hurdle:
Summing over all possible leaf-branching tree topologies \((T,b)\) introduces combinatorial entropy that must be offset by the decay factor \(p^t\). Tight control of the constant \(\lambda\) requires bounding overlap between subtrees.

title: Taxonomy of Proof Approaches
section: 4 3. Naive CDT (No Balancing, No Tree Restriction)
text:
4 3. Naive CDT (No Balancing, No Tree Restriction)
Sources: Notion (CDT No balancing No tree restriction.md), Overleaf (old proofs/proof_old.tex).
Status: Refuted by Counterexample
Key Idea:
Construct \(\mathrm{CDT}(F_1 \vee F_2, \rho)\) by simply evaluating \(F_1\), and on every \(0\)-leaf, appending \(\mathrm{CDT}(F_2, \rho \circ \pi)\) without balancing.






Why It Failed: Jaikumar’s Counterexample



Consider \(F = (X \vee Y) \wedge \bar{Y}\). Under a restriction leaving variables unassigned, the naive construction queries \(X\), and upon branches where \(Y\) loses influence, the tree creates asymmetric paths that fail downward closure and break Cauchy-Schwarz factorization.

title: Taxonomy of Proof Approaches
text:
5 4. Inductive Approach via Path-Variable Factoring
Sources: Obsidian (Indcutive approach.md, New Inductive proof.md), Overleaf (old proofs/inductive_proof.tex).
Status: Stuck / Gap
Key Idea:
Decompose path variables into left and right subformula segments: \[\mathrm{PathVars}_0(F, \rho, a) = (x_{i_1}, \dots, x_{i_s}, x_{i_{s+1}}, \dots, x_{i_t}).\] Assume the first \(s\) variables come from \(F_1\) and the remaining \(t-s\) from \(F_2\), and factor: \[\Pr[\mathcal{E}_t] = \sum_s \Pr[\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{left}}(s)] \cdot \Pr[\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{right}}(t-s) \mid \mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{left}}(s)].\]
Why It Got Stuck:
The conditioning event \(\Delta_t\) depends on the entire sequence of variables \(x_{i_1}, \dots, x_{i_t}\). When unravelling the conditional probability: \[\Delta_{t-1} \text{ depends on } \ell_t \text{ and } x_{i_1}, \dots, x_{i_t},\] the conditioning introduces statistical dependence across restriction steps, preventing clean product factorization without an exponential loss.

title: Taxonomy of Proof Approaches
section: 6 5. Bottom-Up vs. Top-Open KW Protocol Matrix
text:
6 5. Bottom-Up vs. Top-Open KW Protocol Matrix
Sources: Notion (Hastads Base case proof.md), Overleaf (old proofs/bottom_open.tex, old proofs/top_open.tex, old proofs/communication_game.tex).
Status: Partial Success (Base Case Only)
Key Idea:
Represent the formula as a communication game matrix \(M_F\) with monochromatic rectangles \(A_\ell \times B_\ell\). - Bottom-Open: Opens the communication protocol starting from the leaves. - Top-Open: Opens the protocol starting from the root gate.
Outcome:
Proves the base case (\(t=1\)) with optimal bound \(O(p\sqrt{L})\). However, extending to \(t \ge 2\) requires composing protocols across sequential queries, where rectangle monochromaticity degrades into non-monochromatic combinatorial mixtures.

title: Counterexamples & Theoretical Hurdles
text:
Source: Notion (Jaikumars counter example.md), Correspondence with Jaikumar Radhakrishnan (JKR).


Consider the DeMorgan formula: \[F = (X \vee Y) \wedge \bar{Y}\]



When evaluating \(F\) under a restriction \(\rho\) where variables remain unassigned (\(*\)): 1. In a naive CDT construction, one first queries \(X\). 2. If \(X = 0\), the formula simplifies to \(Y \wedge \bar{Y} \equiv 0\). 3. If \(X = 1\), the formula becomes \((1 \vee Y) \wedge \bar{Y} = 1 \wedge \bar{Y} = \bar{Y}\). 4. Under naive concatenation, a path may branch on a variable that has no remaining influence on the output of the full formula, producing asymmetric paths: - A \(0\)-path might explore \(\{X, Y\}\), while the corresponding \(1\)-path explores a completely disjoint or asymmetric set of variables. - This destroys the downward closure property essential for switching lemma style encoding arguments.




“As we build our decision trees, we set variables and consider the remaining formula subject to the setting of variables under the current path. If at some point while building the decision tree, we notice that a variable \(x\) has no influence on the final output, then set \(x\) to \(0\) in the formula. For the rest proceed as before, that is, implement the purple line with no collapsing.”

This insight motivated the modern simultaneous balancing algorithm developed in New CDT.md and contents.tex.

title: Counterexamples & Theoretical Hurdles
text:
2 2. Subformula Simplification vs. CDT Depth 1
Source: Obsidian (July 28 Criticality Meeting.md).






Crucial Meeting Remark (July 28)



A subformula simplifying to a single literal and its CDT having depth 1 are not the same thing!



2.1 Example
Let: \[F = (x_1 \vee x_2) \wedge (x_3 \vee x_4)\] Under a restriction \(\rho\), suppose the subformula \(F_1 = (x_1 \vee x_2)\) simplifies to a literal \(x_1\) (e.g., \(x_2 \to 0\)). However, the decision tree for \(F\) must still evaluate the relation between \(F_1\) and \(F_2\): - \(\mathrm{CDT}(F_1|_\rho)\) has depth 1. - But \(\mathrm{CDT}(F|_\rho)\) depends on the outcome of \(F_1\): if \(x_1 = 0\), the AND gate evaluates to \(0\) immediately; if \(x_1 = 1\), it must proceed to evaluate \((x_3 \vee x_4)\). - Conflating literal reduction with decision tree termination leads to inaccurate depth accounting in inductive steps.

title: Counterexamples & Theoretical Hurdles
text:
3 3. The Inter-Step Conditioning Barrier
Source: Obsidian (Indcutive approach.md), Notion (Criticality of DeMorgan formulae.md).
When expressing the probability of high CDT depth as a sum over path variables: \[\sum_{x_{i_1}, \dots, x_{i_t}} \sum_{\ell_1, \dots, \ell_t} \sqrt{\Pr[A_{F_{-i}} \mid \Delta_i] \cdot \Pr[B_{F_{-i}} \mid \Delta_i]}\]

The condition \(\Delta_t\) depends on \((x_{i_1}, \dots, x_{i_t})\).
The prior condition \(\Delta_{t-1}\) depends on \(\ell_t\) and \((x_{i_1}, \dots, x_{i_{t-1}})\).
Because \(\Delta_t\) and \(\Delta_{t-1}\) share dependencies through the chosen variables, one cannot factor the expectation \(\mathbb{E}[\cdot \mid \Delta_t]\) without accumulating cross-variable covariance terms.

title: Preliminaries & Foundations
text:
A DeMorgan formula \(F\) over variable set \(V = \{x_1, \dots, x_n\}\) is a binary tree where internal nodes are labeled with \(\wedge\) (AND) or \(\vee\) (OR) gates and leaves are labeled with literals from \(\{x_1, \dots, x_n, \bar{x}_1, \dots, \bar{x}_n\}\).
The size of \(F\), denoted \(L(F)\), is the number of leaves in \(F\).


A restriction \(\rho \in \{0, 1, *\}^V\) assigns each variable \(x_i\) independently: \[\rho(x_i) = \begin{cases} * & \text{with probability } p, \\ 0 & \text{with probability } \frac{1-p}{2}, \\ 1 & \text{with probability } \frac{1-p}{2}. \end{cases}\]
The restricted formula \(F|_\rho\) is obtained by substituting values assigned by \(\rho\) and applying standard Boolean simplifications (\(0 \wedge y = 0\), \(1 \vee y = 1\), etc.).

title: Preliminaries & Foundations
text:
2 2. Canonical Decision Trees (CDT)
Given a formula \(F\) and a restriction \(\rho\), a Decision Tree \(\mathrm{DT}(F|_\rho)\) deterministically queries variables until the function value is determined.
A Canonical Decision Tree \(\mathrm{CDT}(F, \rho)\) provides a canonical exploration order for \(F|_\rho\):

Leaf / Literal base case: If \(F = x_i\) and \(\rho(x_i) = *\), the tree queries \(x_i\). If \(\rho(x_i) \in \{0,1\}\), it returns a leaf labeled with that constant.
Recursive combination: For \(F = F_1 \vee F_2\):

First construct \(\mathrm{CDT}(F_1, \rho)\).
For every leaf of \(\mathrm{CDT}(F_1, \rho)\) reaching output \(0\), attach \(\mathrm{CDT}(F_2, \rho \circ \pi)\), where \(\pi\) is the path assignment from the root to that leaf.
For leaves reaching output \(1\), the OR gate is satisfied and evaluation terminates.

title: Preliminaries & Foundations
text:
3 3. Håstad’s Base Case Proof
In Notion (Hastads Base case proof.md), the base case (\(t=1\)) is handled via the Karchmer-Wigderson communication matrix:
Let \(M_F\) be the communication matrix of the game where: \[\text{Rows} = \{\rho : F|_\rho \equiv 0\}, \quad \text{Columns} = \{\rho : F|_\rho \equiv 1\}.\]
For each leaf \(\ell \in F\), let \(A_\ell \times B_\ell\) denote the monochromatic combinatorial rectangle in the KW protocol for \(F\). The set of bad restrictions is bounded by: \[\sum_{\ell \in \mathrm{Leaves}(F)} \sqrt{\Pr[A_\ell] \cdot \Pr[B_\ell]} \le O(p \sqrt{L(F)}).\]
